targets.title: Assessing individual contributions to software engineering projects with Git Logs and user stories.
targets.evidence_quote: In this paper, we explore these questions through a replication of the Buffardi study.
targets.outcome_quote:
Mirroring Buffardi’s analysis, we next conducted a multiple regression analysis to deter­
mine whether the (objective) GitHub metrics (Relative Commit Share, Relative Line Change
Share, Relative Story Share, and Relative Story Point Share) predict the (subjective) CATME
Peer Contribution Rating. In line with Buffardi’s findings, our regression model was signifi­
cant (F(2, 54) = 12.45, p < .001, R2 = .32, R2Adjusted = .29). However, whereas Buffardi’s analysis
found that Relative Commit Share was the significant predictor in the model, we found that
both Relative Line Change Share (Beta = .51, t(56) = 4.43, p < .001) and Relative Story Point
Share (Beta = .24, t(56) = 2.03, p < .05) were the significant predictors.
targets.outcome_reasoning: The authors confirm some findings and explicitly contrast others: the regression model is significant in line with Buffardi, but significant predictors differ. The paper repeatedly calls this a partial or near complete replication, without an overall unqualified success verdict.

reasoning: PDF title, DOI, four authors and page boundaries 335–354 verified. Complete paper including references inspected. A new sample across three institutions re-tests Buffardi (2020); the word robustness refers to generalization with new data, so this is replication. One target paper despite multiple courses, measures and regression models.
